summary.text: 系 is interpreted in one paleographic account as a hand holding connected silk, suggesting binding or connection. Its early graphic analysis remains disputed; later uses include lineage, while “system” is a recorded current gloss.

formation.text: One interpretation of the early forms is pictographic: a hand holds connected strands of silk. The received Shuowen account instead parses 糸 with 丿 as a sound element; another proposal links 系 to 攣. The analyses remain unresolved. The selected seal-script image is a modern redraw, not evidence of a sequence of forms.

components.text: 糸 is identified as thread in the received analysis and as silk in the proposed hand-and-strands interpretation. In that proposed scene it depicts the material being held; the received analysis treats it as a sound element, not a meaning marker.

history.text: Reported oracle-bone and bronze forms are interpreted as a hand holding connected silk. The received Shuowen parsing and a separate proposal linking 系 to 攣 differ from that account. The selected seal-script glyph is a modern redraw, not a dated artifact, and does not establish a sequence of forms.

系 is explicitly assigned a phonetic role within 係. 系, 係, and 繫 are also recorded as counterparts or variants in some contexts, but the evidence does not establish a single graphic chronology or show that 系 regularly arose by simplifying 繫.

Reported early uses include ritual and place or state names, and a bronze personal name. A Warring States text is reported to use 系 for 奚; the evidence gives neither the older word’s sound nor a sound comparison that would establish why this graph was used.

uncertainties.text: The proposed hand-and-silk picture, the received analysis of 糸 plus phonetic 丿, and the proposed link to 攣 remain competing accounts of 系’s graphic origin.
The reported ritual, place or state, and personal-name uses are not dated here as attestations of the lexical meanings thread, connection, lineage, or system.
The readings cited for 系 and 係 support a documented phonetic role for 系 in 係, but their distinct reconstructed forms do not resolve the precise historical sound relation.

senses.text: Thread is a recorded gloss and fits the interpretation of silk held by a hand. The evidence does not identify it as the earliest attested lexical use.
Binding or connection is proposed as the sense of a hand holding connected silk. This is an interpretation of the graph’s origin, not a dated earliest use.

senses.period: historical; cited in a Han-dynasty text
senses.text: A source proposes an extension from connection to lineage and cites a Han-dynasty example, but intermediate stages are not documented.
System is a recorded modern gloss. Its historical development is not shown by this evidence.

senses.gloss: use of 系 to write 奚
senses.text: A Warring States use of 系 for 奚 is reported. This is a proposed reuse of the graph for another word, not a meaning developing from 系. The older word’s sound and any sound match are not given.

developments.text: An extension from connection to lineage is proposed and illustrated with a Han-dynasty example, but intermediate stages are not documented.

limitations.text: The reported ritual, place or state, and personal-name uses are not established here as dated attestations of the listed lexical senses.
No chronology or semantic development for the modern gloss system is supplied.

overview.text: 系 is currently glossed “system.” One proposed origin pictures a hand holding connected silk, suggesting binding or connection; this interpretation remains disputed against another analysis of its early form.

components.text: In the proposed picture, 糸 depicts the connected strands of silk held by a hand.

relationships.text: 糸 depicts the silk strands in the proposed picture of a hand holding connected silk; the received Shuowen analysis instead treats it as part of a phonetic parsing.

系 is documented as the phonetic element in 係. Their modern Mandarin readings are both xì; in the supplied Baxter–Sagart data, 系 is MC hejH, OC *[m]-kˤek-s, while 係 is MC kejH, OC *kˤek-s. The distinct reconstructed forms do not settle the precise historical sound relation.
